summary: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The Wealth Tax Officer, on appeal, held that the assessee was entitled to the wealth tax on the net wealth of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on reference, held that there was no material on the record to show that the assessee had any real or substantial income from the assets of the assessee and that the assessee could not be assessed to wealth Tax. The High Court, in reference, held against the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the Wealth Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the assessee under section 4(1) of the Wealth Tax, 1957, and that the Wealth tax Officer had no power to assess the wealth tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Wealth Tax officer had jurisdiction to assess a person under section 4 of the Wealth tax Act, 1957, as the assessee was a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The Wealth tax Officer was not competent to assess the person under section 3 of the Wealth Act, 1957 as the assessee had no income from the property. [801 D] The Wealth Tax Act is a special law for the assessment of wealth tax. The Wealth Act, however, does not provide for any machinery for assessment of wealth. The Wealth 'tax Officer has no power to determine the wealth of the Hindu undivided family. [802 D] The wealth tax officer had no power under section 4 to assess the income of the assessee under the Wealth tax. The wealth tax Officer had jurisdiction to determine the net wealth. The wealth Tax Officer had jurisdiction under section 4, to assess the net wealth, which was the subject matter of the Wealth, and the wealth tax Officer was competent to assess. [803 D E] The Wealth tax officer had jurisdiction under the Wealth Act to assess the value of the assets of a Hindu undivided Family. The Wealthtax Officer had jurisdiction in the matter. The Wealth, tax Officer had power to assess a Hindu undividedfamily. The Wealth-tax Officer had no authority to assess the assets of any Hindu undivided family in the hands of the assessee, and the Wealth Tax officer was not competent under section 4. [804 D E]

The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant company was registered as a company under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The appellant was registered as an individual and the appellant company was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant 's factory was situated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellant had a factory in the State. The appellant started manufacturing and selling the products of the company. The appellant claimed that it was entitled to exemption under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The appellant contended that the exemption was not available to the appellant under section 4 of the Act and that the appellant was not entitled to exemption. The appellant also contended that the appellant had not been able to establish that the goods were not covered by the relevant entry in the State Act. The High Court held that the appellant 's goods were covered by the entry in the Central Act and that they were covered by entry No. 4 of the State Act and that, therefore, the appellant was entitled to the exemption. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant could not be said to be a dealer in the goods covered by the Central Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appellant was not a dealer in goods covered by entry 4 of the Central Act, and, therefore, it was not entitled under section 4 to the exemption under section 3 of the Central Sales Tax Act. [801 G] The appellant was a manufacturer of the products of its own and the appellant was a dealer in those products. The appellant did not have any other manufacturer of the product. The appellant could not, therefore, be said to have been engaged in the manufacture of the products. [802 G] The fact that the appellant did not manufacture the products of his own would not make it a dealer in them. The appellant would be entitled to the benefit of the exemption under the Central Act in respect of the goods covered under entry 4 of State Act. [702 G]

The petitioner, a company engaged in the business of quarrying and extracting minerals, entered into a contract with the State of Gujarat for the supply of minor minerals to the petitioner. The petitioner was a minor mineral and the petitioner was the State of Bombay. The petitioner 's writ petition challenging the levy of royalty was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not a minor mineral within the meaning of Article 301 of the Constitution and that the levy of the royalty was not in the nature of a tax on the sale or purchase of mineral. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The levy of royalty is not a tax on sale or purchase. The levy is not a fee on the sale of mineral. The levy does not amount to a tax on mineral rights. The levy cannot be a tax on minerals. The levy must be a tax directly on mineral rights and not on mineral rights or on mineral rights, as the levy is not on mineral right. [839 F] 2. The levy in the present case is not a levy on mineral rights but a tax on royalty. The levy was not a tax directly upon mineral rights. [840 A] 3. The levy, therefore, is not a cess on mineral rights as the levy does not on mineral Rights. [841 B]

In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The appellant was entitled under the terms of the trust deed to succeed to his office. The trustees were not entitled to succeed. The appellant had no right to the office. The trust was not a trust. The appellant could not succeed to the post of trustee. [839 C] (2) The appellant had not been appointed a hereditary trustees. [840 C] (3) The appellant could be removed from the office by the trustee only on the ground of misconduct or incapacity. The appellant firm was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his wife, the wife and the minor sons. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the firm to tax in the hands of the family. The Income Tax Officer, however, assessed the income to tax in respect of the income of a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income of an assessee was not liable to be taxed in the hands Of the family but was liable to be assessed in the hands and that the income was not liable for the income of any other person. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that the Income Tax Officer was not entitled to assess the income of his wife and that the Income tax Officer was not competent to assess the Income tax. The High Court in reference held that the Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the income from the firm was liable to tax in view of the provisions of section 10(2) of the Act. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The words "as the case may be" in section 10(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922, are wide enough to include within their scope the income from which income is derived. The words " as the case may" in section 9(1) are wide enough not to include within its scope the income of one person but include income from other sources. The words are wide enough so as to include within it all the income from other source. The words must be read in the context of the words " as if the income from any other source" in section 2(1) and the words "as if the income of such other source" are used in the context. [864 D] (ii) The words 'as the case might be ' in section 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1922 are wide enough, to include within the scope of the words 'as if the Income tax officer 's order. The words ' as the case might ' in section 9 (1) are not to be read in isolation but are to be read as if the words ' as if the Income Tax officer 's orders. [865 E] (iii) The words in the context in which they occur are not to include income from the assets of the Hindu undivided family. The words in section 10 (1) of that Act are wide enough in the context to include within them all the income of that family. [867 D]

The workmen claimed that the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal was not justified. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to the minimum wage of Rs. 2,000 per day. The Tribunal also held that the minimum wages of the workmen were not at all higher than the minimum wage. The Tribunal, however, held that the Company was entitled to the maximum wage of Rs 2,000. The Tribunal further held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen had been paid less than the minimum wages fixed by the award. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right when it held that the company was entitled to minimum wage of the workmen. The Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was not entitled to the basic wage of Rs 1,000. [848 E] (ii) The Tribunal had erred in holding that there was no minimum wage of workmen. The Company was entitled only to the minimum wages. The Tribunal had not considered the question whether the minimum wage was fixed by the company. The Tribunal did not consider the question whether there was any minimum wage of wages. The Company had not been able to show that the minimum was fixed by it. The Tribunal has not considered whether the minimum was to be fixed by the Company. [849 F] (iii) The Tribunal has found that the minimum fixed by the appellant company was not at all lower than the minimum fixed. The Tribunal found that the Company had not fixed any minimum wage. It was also found that the workmen did not pay the minimum wages and the minimum wages were fixed by the Award. The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1939. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the sales of cotton and cotton. The appellant contended that the sales tax authorities had no jurisdiction to assess the sales tax on sales of cotton. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the contention and held that the sales were not taxable. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed. The appellant then applied to the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal for a reference of the questions of law arising out of the order of the Sales Tax Officer. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not liable to pay sales tax on cotton and cotton and that the sales of the cotton and cotton were not taxable under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales tax Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the Sales Tax Tribunal had jurisdiction to determine the question of law arising in the case. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. The question was whether the sales of a registered dealer were taxable under section 2(a) of the Act. Held, that the sales in question were not taxable because the sales were effected by the registered dealer to whom the goods were sold and the sales were therefore taxable. The sales were not sales within the meaning of section 2(b) and were not taxable at all. The sales in question did not come within the purview of section 8(b) but were sales in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The sales of the appellant were not sales in the State of Bombay. The sales did not come under the purview of the Bombay General Sales Tax Act. The sales could not be said to be sales in the sense of the word "sale" in section 2(c) of the . The sales were in the course, of inter State commerce and were not sales of the same kind as the sales in the case of other dealers. The sales fell under the purview and the sales in respect of the same goods were not taxable in the State. The sales, therefore, were not sales. The sales had been made by the registered dealers to the registered dealers and the sales had been effected by the unregistered dealers to the unregistered dealers. The Sales tax authorities were right in holding that the sales had taken place outside the State of Madras. The sales having taken place outside Madras, the sales were outside the State.

The appellant was a lessee of the land in question. The lease was for a period of 20 years. The lease expired on March 31, 1949. The appellant 's application for renewal of the lease was rejected by the Collector on the ground that the lease was not for a period exceeding 20 years. On appeal the Collector held that the lease had been terminated by the appellant on the ground of the breach of the conditions of the lease. The appellant appealed to the Board of Revenue. The Board held that the appellant was not entitled to the renewal of the first lease. The Board, however, held that the first lease was for the period of 20. years and that the appellant had not been given a fresh lease. The Collector held that there was no subsisting lease and that the lease in question was not for the period for which the lease was granted. The appellant then applied to the Board for renewal of his lease. The State Government rejected the appellant 's contention that the lease having been terminated by him, the appellant was entitled to the grant of the lease in his favour. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the second lease was for more than 20 years and that it was not for any period exceeding 20. years. The appellant contended that the lease for a period not exceeding 20 years was for a further period of 20, that the lease could not be renewed for a period longer than 20 years. Held, that the appellant ' was entitled to renewal of the second lease for a further term of 20 years and the appellant was also entitled to the same renewal for a further further period of 21 years. The High court was in error in holding that the appellant could not be granted the renewal of a lease for a longer period than 20 years, and that the renewal of lease for a lesser period was not for an indefinite period. The appellant was not a lessee for a lesser term. The appellant had not obtained a lease for more than 10 years. The first lease was not a lease for the whole of the lease for the entire period. The second lease was not an extension of the lease and the second lease could not, therefore, be renewed for any period beyond 20 years.
